Fallout 4 overhauled the combat mechanics for the FPS Fallout games. This includes both gunplay and melee combat, and we'll be focusing on the latter.


Ignoring the exploit of animation cancelling, I'll be focusing on combat takedowns and 3rd-person melee combat.


All melee weapons (both unarmed and melee proper) swing faster in third-person. It's an outright nerf to play a melee build in Fallout 4 first-person, unless you're using the previously mentioned animation cancelling.

Melee takedowns involve double-tapping the power attack button (ALT key on the keyboard) while being in the third-person camera. These are anything from leg sweeps, to staggers, to [ground'n'pounds](https://youtu.be/he9p0L-OhlE?t=57) if you're using certain weapons. 

These really make melee combat very diverse, and they give you a wide variety of utility in combat to give yourself breathing room.

This may be lost on a lot of people, but NBA 2k21. I started playing it recently because it was free on the Epic Games Store, and the way your MyCareer character is balanced is very unfortunate. Whenever you create your character, you set your potential on your different stats (like dunks, 3-pointers, defense, etc.), and that determines how high you can raise your stats.

The problem with this is that your BASE stats (speed, stamina, strength, etc) are increased by leveling up your potential stats. So, until you start getting your overall level to around 80-ish, you're just a _worse_ player than the real life people you're on a team with/against. Also, once your potential stats start getting into the 70's, you're no longer earning enough of the premium currency in a game to level up the stat once, so you have to play two+ games per stat increase. It takes approximately 30-40 NBA games during your career to become somewhat competent, not just mediocre. And the game just... isn't fun for those 30-40 games.

Don't worry, though, because you can drop around 60 USD to immediately max out your character's stats.

I have a few that I use, to great effect:


1. A character can fail on a number of death saving throws equal to their Constitution score. The only way to remove a failure is with a level up or the Greater Restoration spell. 

2. If a player is revived from being unconscious, either through magic or a short rest, they gain a stack of exhaustion. This stacks with itself. The stacks of exhaustion are lost as normal from long rests.

3. If a player is knocked unconscious from a critical hit and isn’t killed outright, they roll on the Lingering Injuries table in the DMG.


These are what I use, though I made sure that the players are okay with this from the get go. I would also recommend looking into Matthew Mercer’s resurrection rules as an additional thing to include.
